title: Lechon kawali
intro: Pork belly simmered until tender, then deep-fried until the skin puffs and crackles while the meat stays juicy. It is chopped into chunks and dipped in spiced vinegar or lechon sauce.

items.name: pork belly
items.note: one slab with skin, about 2 inches thick

items.name: salt
items.note: for boiling, plus 1 tsp for rubbing

steps.text: Put the pork in a pot with the salt, peppercorns, bay leaves and garlic. Add water to cover by an inch and bring to a boil, skimming off the scum.
Lower the heat, cover and simmer until a fork slides easily into the meat but the slab still holds its shape.
Lift the pork out and pat it completely dry. Rub the skin with 1 tsp salt and leave it on a rack, skin side up, until the surface feels dry to the touch.
Meanwhile, stir together all the dip ingredients and set aside.
Heat the oil in a deep, heavy pot to 350°F (175°C). Pat the pork dry once more and lower it in carefully, skin side down. Cover loosely with a splatter guard or lid set ajar, as the skin pops.
Fry, turning once or twice, until the skin is deep golden and blistered all over.
Drain on a rack so the bottom stays crisp. Let it rest before cutting.
Chop into bite-size pieces with a heavy knife and serve hot with the dip and steamed rice.

tips: For the crispiest skin, refrigerate the boiled pork uncovered overnight before frying. Any water left on the surface makes the oil spit, so dry it well.

title: Crispy pata
intro: A whole pork hock boiled until tender, then deep-fried until the skin is shatteringly crisp and the meat falls off the bone. It is served whole for sharing, with a sharp soy and vinegar dip.

items.name: salt
items.note: for boiling, plus 1 tsp for rubbing

items.name: cooking oil
items.note: enough to cover the hock halfway

steps.text: Put the hock in a large pot with the salt, peppercorns, bay leaves, garlic and onion. Cover with water and bring to a boil, skimming off the scum.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the meat is tender and the skin gives easily when pressed.
Lift the hock out, pat it dry and rub the skin with 1 tsp salt. Leave it on a rack until the skin is completely dry and cool.
Stir together the dip ingredients and set aside.
Heat the oil in a deep, heavy pot to 350°F (175°C). Lower the hock in carefully and cover with a splatter guard or a lid set ajar.
Fry, turning every few minutes, until the skin is deep golden, blistered and crisp all over.
Drain on a rack for a few minutes, then serve whole with kitchen shears or a heavy knife, the dip and steamed rice.

tips: Boil and dry the hock a day ahead and refrigerate it uncovered overnight: the drier the skin, the crisper and safer the fry. A pressure cooker cuts the boiling to about 35 minutes.

title: Bagnet
intro: Ilocano pork belly that is boiled, dried and fried twice, so the skin turns into a thick, bubbly crackling over tender, rendered meat. It is eaten with spiced vinegar or a fresh tomato and onion salad.

items.name: pork belly
items.note: with skin, cut into 3 strips about 2 inches wide

steps.text: Put the pork strips in a pot with the salt, peppercorns, bay leaves and garlic. Cover with water and bring to a boil, skimming off the scum.
Simmer until tender but not falling apart.
Drain, pat dry and rub lightly with salt. Leave on a rack until the surface is dry and the pork is cool.
Heat the oil in a deep, heavy pot to 300°F (150°C). Fry the pork, covered with a splatter guard, until the fat has rendered and the skin turns pale gold.
Lift the pork out and let it cool completely on the rack. Turn off the heat under the oil.
Reheat the oil to 375°F (190°C). Fry the pork again until the skin puffs into small blisters and turns deep golden.
Drain on the rack. Mix the vinegar, garlic and chilies for dipping, and toss the tomatoes with the onion.
Chop the bagnet into thick slices and serve with the vinegar, the tomato salad and rice.

tips: Bagnet is traditionally dried overnight, and the first fry can be done a day ahead: keep the pieces in the fridge and give them the hot second fry just before serving.

title: Humba
intro: Visayan braised pork belly in soy sauce, vinegar and brown sugar with salted black beans and dried banana blossoms. The fat melts into a sticky, sweet and salty sauce that goes with a lot of rice.

items.name: dried banana blossoms
items.note: soaked in water for 15 minutes, knotted

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the pork on all sides in batches. Spoon off all but 2 tbsp of the rendered fat.
Lower the heat and sauté the garlic and onion in the fat until soft.
Return the pork with the soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns. Bring to a boil.
Add the vinegar and let it boil without stirring.
Stir in the brown sugar, cover and simmer over low heat until the pork is very tender, adding a splash of water if it gets dry.
Add the drained banana blossoms and black beans and simmer uncovered until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Taste and adjust with a little more sugar or soy sauce. Serve with steamed rice.

tips: Some families add a cup of pineapple juice in place of part of the water for a fruitier sauce. Humba keeps well and tastes better the next day.

title: Pata tim
intro: Pork hock braised slowly with soy sauce, sugar and star anise until the skin turns soft and glossy and the meat pulls off the bone. It is served in its thick, sweet sauce with shiitake mushrooms and bok choy.

items.name: dried shiitake mushrooms
items.note: soaked in hot water for 20 minutes

steps.text: Put the hock in a pot of boiling water and boil to clean it, then drain and rinse.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and brown the hock lightly on all sides. Add the garlic and cook until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, brown sugar, star anise, peppercorns, bay leaves and water. Bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer over low heat, turning the hock every 30 minutes, until the skin is soft and the meat is very tender.
Add the drained mushrooms and simmer uncovered until the sauce has reduced to about 1.5 cups.
Meanwhile, blanch the bok choy in boiling salted water until bright green, then drain.
Move the hock and mushrooms to a platter. Stir the cornstarch mixture into the sauce and simmer until glossy and thick.
Arrange the bok choy around the hock, pour the sauce over and serve with rice.

tips: A pressure cooker brings the braising time down to about 45 minutes. Skim the fat off the sauce before thickening it if it looks oily.

title: Pork belly hamonado
intro: Thick slices of pork belly simmered in pineapple juice and soy sauce, then cooked down until the sauce turns to a sticky, caramelized glaze. Seared pineapple rings go on top.

items.name: pork belly
items.note: skin on, cut into slices about 1/2 inch thick

steps.text: Put the pork slices in a wide pan with the pineapple juice, soy sauce, garlic, water, bay leaf and pepper. Bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer over low heat until the pork is tender, turning the slices once.
Uncover, stir in the brown sugar and keep simmering until the liquid has almost evaporated and the pork starts to fry in its own fat.
Fry the slices in the glaze, turning often, until sticky and caramelized at the edges. Watch closely, as the sugar burns quickly. Move the pork to a plate.
Sear the pineapple rings in the same pan until browned in spots, then set them on top of the pork and spoon over any glaze left in the pan.
Serve hot with steamed rice.

tips: If the glaze darkens before the pork browns, add 2 tbsp water and lower the heat.

title: Pork ribs hamonado
intro: Pork spareribs braised in pineapple juice, soy sauce and brown sugar until tender, then glazed under the broiler. Sweet, salty and sticky, with meat that pulls off the bone.

steps.text: Put the ribs, pineapple juice, soy sauce, garlic, onion, water and bay leaves in a heavy pot and bring to a boil, skimming off the scum.
Cover and simmer over low heat until the ribs are tender.
Heat the broiler. Move the ribs to a foil-lined baking tray, meaty side up.
Add the brown sugar and banana ketchup to the pot and boil the liquid hard, stirring, until it reduces to a thick glaze, about 1 cup.
Brush the ribs generously with the glaze and broil until bubbling and browned at the edges.
Warm the pineapple chunks in the rest of the glaze, spoon them over the ribs and serve with rice.

tips: Keep an eye on the ribs under the broiler: sugar-heavy glazes go from browned to burnt in under a minute.

title: Pork asado
intro: Chinese-Filipino pork shoulder braised in soy sauce, sugar and star anise, then sliced and served in a thick, sweet and savory sauce. Hard-boiled eggs simmer in the sauce alongside.

steps.text: Pat the pork dry. Heat the oil in a heavy pot and brown the pork well on all sides. Set it aside.
Sauté the garlic and onion in the same pot until soft.
Add the soy sauce, brown sugar, oyster sauce, star anise, five-spice powder and water. Return the pork and bring to a boil.
Cover and simmer over low heat, turning the pork every 20 minutes, until a fork slides in easily.
Add the eggs and simmer uncovered, turning them so they color evenly, while the sauce reduces.
Lift out the pork and let it rest, then slice it about 1/4 inch thick. Halve the eggs.
Stir the cornstarch mixture into the sauce and simmer until glossy. Pour over the sliced pork and eggs and serve with rice.

tips: Leftover asado, chopped with its sauce, makes a good filling for homemade siopao or a topping for fried rice.

title: Lechon macau
intro: Chinese-style roast pork belly with five-spice seasoned meat and a thin, crunchy, bubbled skin. It is sliced into strips and dipped in hoisin, sweet chili or lechon sauce.

steps.text: Pour boiling water over the skin to tighten it, then pat dry. Prick the skin all over with a skewer or the tip of a sharp knife, without cutting into the meat.
Mix the five-spice powder, 1 tsp salt, sugar and garlic and rub it on the meat side and edges only, keeping the skin clean.
Wrap foil around the sides and bottom of the slab like a tray so only the skin shows. Brush the skin with the vinegar and leave it uncovered in the fridge to dry.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Pack the coarse salt over the skin in an even layer and roast on a rack set over a tray.
Lift off and discard the salt crust. Raise the heat to 450°F (230°C) or turn on the broiler.
Roast until the skin puffs and crackles all over, turning the tray so it browns evenly and covering any dark spots with foil.
Rest the pork, then cut into strips and slices with a heavy knife and serve with the sauce.

tips: Drying the skin overnight in the fridge, uncovered, gives an even crisper crackling. Scrape off any burnt bits with a knife rather than discarding the skin.

title: Pininyahang baboy
intro: Pork simmered in pineapple juice with potatoes, carrots and bell peppers, then finished with evaporated milk for a creamy, mildly sweet and tangy sauce. The pork version of pininyahang manok.

steps.text: Toss the pork with half of the pineapple juice and let it sit while you prepare the vegetables.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and sauté the garlic and onion until soft. Add the pork, keeping its juice, and cook until it is no longer pink.
Add the fish sauce and let it sizzle, then pour in the rest of the pineapple juice and the water. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer until the pork is almost tender.
Add the potatoes and carrot and simmer until tender.
Stir in the pineapple chunks, bell pepper, evaporated milk and pepper. Simmer gently, without boiling hard, until the sauce is creamy and the pepper is just soft.
Taste, adding more fish sauce if needed, and serve with rice.

tips: Coconut milk can stand in for the evaporated milk. Keep the heat low once the milk goes in so the sauce does not split.

title: Binagoongang baboy
intro: Pork belly simmered until tender, then cooked down with sautéed shrimp paste, tomatoes and a splash of vinegar. Salty, rich and a little sweet, it is best with plain rice and slices of green mango.

steps.text: Put the pork and water in a wide pan and bring to a boil. Cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Uncover and keep cooking until the water evaporates and the pork starts to fry in its rendered fat. Brown the pieces lightly, then spoon off all but 2 tbsp of fat.
Push the pork aside and sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes in the fat until the tomatoes are soft and mushy.
Stir in the shrimp paste and cook, stirring, until it darkens slightly and smells toasty.
Add the vinegar and let it boil without stirring. Then add the sugar, pepper, chilies and a splash of water.
Simmer, stirring now and then, until the sauce clings to the pork.
Taste: add a pinch of sugar if too salty, more shrimp paste if too mild. Serve with rice.

tips: Brands of bagoong vary a lot in saltiness. Start with less, taste, and add more at the end.

title: Binagoongang baboy with eggplant
intro: Pork belly and shrimp paste with fried eggplant folded in at the end, so the soft eggplant soaks up the salty, savory sauce. A one-pan ulam that stretches a little pork a long way.

steps.text: Put the pork and water in a wide pan, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until tender.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in a frying pan and fry the eggplant in batches until browned and soft. Drain on paper towels.
Uncover the pork and cook until the water evaporates and the pork browns lightly in its own fat. Spoon off excess fat, leaving about 2 tbsp.
Sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes with the pork until the tomatoes break down.
Add the shrimp paste and cook, stirring, until fragrant. Add the vinegar and let it boil without stirring, then add the sugar and a splash of water.
Fold in the fried eggplant and simmer gently until heated through and coated in sauce.
Taste, adjust with sugar or shrimp paste, and serve with rice.

tips: Fry the eggplant skin side down first so it keeps its purple color. Stir gently once it goes in, or it turns to mush.

title: Crispy binagoongan
intro: Crunchy fried pork belly tossed in a quick, garlicky shrimp paste sauce right before serving. You get crackling skin and salty, sweet bagoong in every bite.

steps.text: Put the pork in a pot with the salt, peppercorns and bay leaves, cover with water and bring to a boil. Simmer until tender.
Drain and pat the pork completely dry. Leave it on a rack until the surface feels dry.
Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C) in a deep, heavy pot and fry the pork, covered with a splatter guard, until golden and crisp. Drain on a rack and cut into bite-size pieces.
In a wok, heat 2 tbsp of the frying oil and sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes until soft.
Add the shrimp paste, sugar and chilies and cook, stirring, until fragrant. Add the vinegar and let it bubble without stirring.
Turn off the heat, add the crispy pork and toss quickly to coat. Serve right away so the skin stays crunchy.

tips: Leftover lechon kawali works perfectly here. Reheat it in a hot oven first so it crisps up again before tossing.

title: Pork bistek
intro: Thin slices of pork marinated in soy sauce and calamansi, seared and simmered in the marinade, then topped with soft onion rings. Salty, tangy and peppery, it is an everyday ulam for rice.

steps.text: Mix the pork with the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic and pepper. Let it marinate.
Heat the oil in a wide pan and cook the onion rings until just softened. Set them aside.
Lift the pork out of the marinade, keeping the marinade. Sear the slices in the same pan in batches until browned on both sides.
Return all the pork with the marinade and water. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until tender.
Stir in the sugar if using and simmer uncovered until the sauce is slightly thickened.
Top with the onion rings, warm through and serve with rice.

tips: Partly freezing the pork for 30 minutes makes thin, even slices much easier to cut.

title: Pork steak
intro: Filipino-style bone-in pork chops browned and braised in a soy and calamansi sauce, finished with butter and onion rings. The sauce turns savory, tangy and glossy, perfect spooned over rice.

items.name: bone-in pork chops
items.note: about 3/4 inch thick, 800 g in all

steps.text: Snip the fat on the edge of each chop in two or three places so it does not curl. Marinate the chops in the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic and pepper.
Lift out the chops and pat them dry, keeping the marinade. Heat the oil in a wide pan and brown the chops well on both sides.
Pour in the marinade, water and sugar. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer over low heat until the chops are tender, turning them once.
Move the chops to a plate. Add the onion rings to the pan and cook until just soft.
Swirl in the butter until the sauce is glossy, then pour the onions and sauce over the chops and serve with rice.

tips: Thicker chops need a few more minutes of simmering. Add a splash of water if the sauce reduces too far.

title: Pork barbecue
intro: Thin slices of pork marinated in soy sauce, banana ketchup, soda and calamansi, threaded onto bamboo skewers and grilled with a sweet basting sauce. Sticky, smoky and slightly charred at the edges.

steps.text: Mix all the marinade ingredients in a bowl, add the pork and toss to coat. Cover and refrigerate.
Thread 4 or 5 slices onto each soaked skewer, folding the slices so they bunch up a little.
Pour the leftover marinade into a small pan with the ketchup and oil for basting. Boil it, stirring, until slightly thickened.
Grill the skewers over medium-hot charcoal, turning and basting every couple of minutes, until cooked through and charred in spots.
Serve hot with rice and a dip of vinegar with chopped onion and chili.

tips: Marinate overnight for the best flavor. A grill pan or the broiler works too; line the tray with foil, as the sugary sauce burns onto pans.

title: Inihaw na liempo
intro: Pork belly slices marinated in soy sauce, calamansi and garlic, then grilled until the fat crisps and the edges char. Chopped and dipped in spiced soy and vinegar, it is a weekend grill favorite.

steps.text: Mix the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, brown sugar and pepper. Toss the pork slices in it, cover and refrigerate.
Light a charcoal grill and let the coals burn down to medium heat. Mix the dip ingredients.

Lift the pork out of the marinade and shake off the garlic bits, which burn easily. Grill, turning every few minutes and brushing with marinade during the first 10 minutes only, until cooked through and crisp at the edges.
Rest the slices for a couple of minutes, then cut into strips.
Serve with the dip, rice and grilled eggplant or a tomato and onion salad.

tips: Move the slices away from flare-ups: dripping pork fat catches fire quickly. Overnight marinating gives a deeper flavor.

title: Pork inasal
intro: Grilled pork in the Bacolod inasal style, marinated in vinegar, calamansi, lemongrass and ginger and basted with garlicky annatto oil. Tangy, smoky and bright orange, eaten with garlic rice and spiced vinegar.

steps.text: Mix all the marinade ingredients, add the pork and toss well. Cover and refrigerate.
Warm the oil with the annatto seeds over low heat until deep orange. Strain out the seeds, stir in the garlic and a pinch of salt, and keep warm.
Thread the pork onto the skewers. Mix a few spoonfuls of the marinade into the annatto oil for basting.
Grill over medium-hot charcoal, turning and basting with the annatto oil every few minutes, until cooked through and charred at the edges.
Serve with garlic rice, calamansi and a dip of vinegar with chilies.

tips: For the classic flavor, marinate overnight. Keep basting right to the end: it is what gives inasal its color.

title: Inihaw na pork chop
intro: Pork chops marinated in soy sauce, calamansi, garlic and a little oyster sauce, then grilled until smoky and caramelized. Serve with rice and atchara.

steps.text: Snip the fat on the edge of each chop so it stays flat. Mix the soy sauce, calamansi juice, oyster sauce, brown sugar, garlic and pepper, coat the chops and refrigerate.
Heat a charcoal grill to medium. Lift the chops out of the marinade and stir the oil into what is left for basting.
Grill the chops, basting now and then, until browned and cooked through, about 6 minutes per side.
Rest the chops for a few minutes, then serve with rice and atchara.

tips: A grill pan over medium heat works too. Lower the heat if the sugar chars before the meat is cooked.

title: Inihaw na tadyang
intro: Pork spareribs simmered until tender, then grilled over charcoal with a sweet soy and banana ketchup glaze. Smoky, sticky and soft enough to pull off the bone.

items.name: pork spareribs
items.note: cut into slabs of 3 or 4 ribs

steps.text: Put the ribs, onion, garlic, bay leaves and salt in a pot, cover with water and bring to a boil, skimming off the scum.
Simmer until the ribs are tender but not falling apart.
Meanwhile, mix all the glaze ingredients in a small pan and simmer until slightly thickened.
Drain the ribs and pat them dry. Brush both sides with the glaze and let them sit while the charcoal heats to medium.
Grill the ribs, turning and brushing with more glaze every couple of minutes, until browned and charred at the edges.
Cut between the bones and serve with rice and a soy-vinegar dip.

tips: The boiling liquid makes a good broth for soup or for cooking rice. The ribs can be boiled a day ahead and grilled straight from the fridge.

title: Lechon paksiw
intro: Leftover roast pork simmered in vinegar and lechon sauce until soft and coated in a sweet, tangy, liver-thickened sauce. The usual way to finish the lechon the day after a party.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot and sauté the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the pork, water, soy sauce, bay leaves and peppercorns and bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring.
Stir in the lechon sauce and brown sugar. Cover and simmer over low heat, stirring now and then so it does not stick, until the pork is soft and the skin is tender.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce is thick enough to coat the pork.
Taste and add a little more sugar or vinegar to balance. Serve with rice.

tips: No lechon sauce? Mash 3 tbsp liver spread with 2 tbsp breadcrumbs and an extra tablespoon of sugar into the sauce. Like most paksiw, it keeps for days and tastes better reheated.

title: Paksiw na pata
intro: Pork hock slices braised slowly in vinegar, soy sauce and brown sugar with dried banana blossoms until the skin turns soft and sticky. Sweet and sour, rich, and made for rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot and sauté the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the pork, soy sauce, water, bay leaves and peppercorns. Bring to a boil and skim off the scum.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring.
Stir in the brown sugar. Cover and simmer over low heat until the skin is soft and the meat is very tender, turning the pieces now and then and adding water if it gets dry.
Add the drained banana blossoms and simmer uncovered until the sauce reduces and turns sticky.
Taste, adjust with sugar or vinegar, and serve with steamed rice.

tips: Ask the butcher to slice the pata for you; the bone is hard to cut at home. A pressure cooker cuts the braising time to about 40 minutes.

title: Fried pork chop
intro: Thin pork chops marinated in calamansi, soy sauce and garlic, then pan-fried until golden with crisp, rendered edges. Simple everyday ulam, eaten with rice and banana ketchup or a soy-calamansi dip.

steps.text: Snip the fat on the edge of each chop in two places so it stays flat. Rub the chops with the calamansi juice, soy sauce, garlic, salt and pepper and let them marinate.
Scrape off the garlic bits and pat the chops very dry with paper towels.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Fry the chops without moving them until the underside is golden brown.
Turn and fry the other side until golden and cooked through, with no pink at the bone.
Drain briefly on paper towels and serve hot with rice and your dip of choice.

tips: Cover the pan loosely with a splatter guard: the soy marinade makes the oil spit. A fried egg and garlic rice turn this into a full breakfast too.

title: Breaded pork chop
intro: Pork chops pounded thin, coated in flour, egg and breadcrumbs, and fried until crunchy and golden. Kids love them with rice and banana ketchup.

steps.text: Pound the chops between sheets of plastic wrap to an even 1/4 inch. Season with the salt, pepper, garlic powder and calamansi juice.
Set out the flour, beaten eggs and breadcrumbs in three shallow plates. Coat each chop in flour, then egg, then breadcrumbs, pressing so the crumbs stick.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat until a crumb sizzles right away.
Fry the chops two at a time until deep golden on the first side.
Turn and fry until the second side is golden and the pork is cooked through.
Drain on a rack or paper towels and serve with rice and banana ketchup.

tips: Letting the breaded chops sit in the fridge for 15 minutes before frying helps the coating stay on.

title: Pork chop with mushroom gravy
intro: Pan-fried pork chops smothered in a brown mushroom gravy made from the pan drippings. Savory and comforting, it is the kind of plate you get at a Filipino diner, with rice to catch the gravy.

steps.text: Snip the fat on the edge of each chop and season both sides with the salt, pepper and garlic powder.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and fry the chops until browned and cooked through, about 5 minutes per side. Set them aside on a plate.
Lower the heat to medium and melt the butter in the same pan. Cook the onion and mushrooms until the mushrooms are browned.
Sprinkle in the flour and stir until it smells nutty and turns light brown.
Whisk in the broth a little at a time, then add the soy sauce and Worcestershire. Simmer, stirring, until the gravy thickens.
Return the chops and their juices to the pan and simmer, spooning the gravy over, until heated through.
Taste the gravy for salt and serve with rice.

tips: If the gravy gets too thick, loosen it with a splash of water. Scrape up the browned bits in the pan: they are where the flavor is.
